newsitem.title: USA: U.S. clears way for charges against diplomat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. clears way for charges against diplomat.

text.p: The State Department said it notified U.S. justice authorities on Tuesday that Georgia had waived immunity for a diplomat involved in a fatal car crash in Washington, clearing the way for charges against him.
Spokesman Glyn Davies said the department had sent a letter to the office of U.S. Attorney Eric Holder formally advising it of last week's decision by the former Soviet republic.

Gueorgui Makharadze allegedly triggered a five-car crash on Jan. 4 when his vehicle, travelling at an estimated 80 mph (130 kph), slammed into a stationary car at a red light at Dupont Circle in the heart of Washington.
The accident killed Joviane Waltrick, a 16-year-old Brazilian girl living in Kensington, Maryland, a Washington suburb. Police say alcohol may have played a role.

"What we're doing today is sending a letter to the Office of the U.S. Attorney informing the U.S. attorney that the government of Georgia has waived immunity," said Davies, who later confirmed that the letter had been sent.
"What we'd like to do at this stage is thank the government of Georgia for its very close cooperation right from the start in what has been a very tragic matter."

Makharadze, 35, was his country's No. 2 diplomat in Washington and a rising star in the Georgian foreign service, making the waiver decision a hard one for President Eduard Shevardnadze. Prosecutors are now expected to seek a grand jury indictment charging Makharadze with involuntary manslaughter. The charges carry a maximum penalty of up to 30 years in prison.

Newsweek magazine has reported that tests at Georgetown University Hospital, taken several hours after the accident, showed that Makharadze had a blood alcohol level far above the legally drunk level.

Shevardnadze suggested in a radio interview on Monday that Makharadze, if convicted, might serve his term in Georgia rather than the United States and said there would be "serious negotiations" with Washington on this.

But Davies said that, so far, he was "not aware that the issue was even raised by the government of Georgia." He also said Georgia was not at present a party to the Strasbourg Convention, an international treaty on prisoner transfers. "So even if it came to consideration of an issue like that, there would be a fair amount of work that would have to be done."
